Subject: DRAFT — Wellsford Road: how our collision count went wrong

By Nell Garside

On 2 November, we reported that Wellsford Road had the highest number of recorded injury collisions of any road in Bristol over the five years from 2021 to 2025. We put the figure at 41. That was wrong. The correct number is 23, placing Wellsford Road sixth.

The corrected table has been online since Friday 6 November, with a correction on the original article. But a note at the bottom of that article is not a sufficient account of what happened. The story received more than 48,000 page views, and the incorrect figure travelled well beyond our website.

Residents were entitled to expect us to check it properly before publication. I am sorry for the concern our error caused, particularly among parents asking whether it was safe to walk their children to Wellsford Primary. The responsibility belongs to the Data Desk. Our checks failed to catch a mistake in our analysis.

What went wrong

Our analysis uses Department for Transport records of collisions in which at least one person was injured, covering roads within the city council boundary.

The error occurred when we joined the collision records to the road information used to produce the table. That process duplicated some collision–road pairs: the same collision appeared twice in the tally for the same road. We counted those repeated entries when we should have counted each collision only once per road.

On Wellsford Road, removing 18 duplicate entries reduced the total from 41 to 23. Those 18 entries were not additional collisions. They were repeat entries for collisions already counted.

We have corrected the calculation so that each unique accident index, the identifier attached to a collision record, is counted once per road. We then reran the whole citywide table, rather than simply changing Wellsford Road’s figure.

The corrected leading six roads are:

1. Kingsmere Road: 32 injury collisions
2. Alder Hill: 31
3. Tanner’s Way: 28
4. Crossfield Road: 26
5. Hambrook Lane: 24
6. Wellsford Road: 23

Why the distinction matters

The Fishponds Streets Forum told us that a member had worked through the published Department for Transport data herself and could not reproduce our figure of 41. She was right to challenge it. Readers should not have to reconstruct our analysis to discover an error, but that challenge deserved a proper answer.

Of the 23 recorded injury collisions on Wellsford Road, three were classified as serious and none was fatal. The description circulating locally of it as Bristol’s “deadliest road” is not supported by these figures.

That does not mean the road is safe, or that residents’ concerns can be dismissed. Twenty-three injury collisions remain 23 injury collisions. A ranked count does not, on its own, establish how safe a particular walk to school is. It does not account for how many people use each road or describe the conditions at every crossing and junction. We should not turn a correction to an overstated figure into reassurance the data cannot provide.

What changes now

From now on, we will publish the cleaned data and the code used to produce our ranked tables alongside them, so readers can inspect how the figures were calculated. A second analyst will independently reproduce each ranked table before publication. A table will not run until that check is complete.

These are checks we should have had in place for this story. Publishing the method will not remove our responsibility for getting it right; it will make our work more open to scrutiny.

I would also like to take up the invitation to attend the Fishponds Streets Forum meeting at Fishponds Library on 17 November at 7pm, to explain the correction and answer residents’ questions in person. Those who challenged the figure were owed more than a changed number. They were owed an explanation of how we arrived at it, why it was wrong and what we will do differently.
